title: Quarto draft — preview notes
text:
This is a draft Quarto build of the portfolio, living alongside the existing Jekyll site so nothing breaks while we iterate.


From inside this folder:
cd quarto
quarto preview
That’ll open it at http://localhost:<port> and live-reload as files change. Quit with Ctrl-C.
If you don’t have Quarto installed yet:
brew install --cask quarto




index.qmd — homepage. Hero karyotype, tagline, three “what I do” lines, three featured work cards, footer.
about.qmd — the real story. Short version, “why now,” what I bring, lived-experience note.
work/index.qmd — samples landing.
samples/*.qmd — your three existing genomics samples, ported.
assets/karyotype.svg — the hero. A stylized 23-pair karyotype I drew in SVG. Swap it for a real spectral-karyotype image when we find or commission one — just replace the file at the same path.
assets/headshot.jpg — copied from the Escaping academia folder.
styles.scss — palette, typography, layout. All the visual decisions live here.
_quarto.yml — site config (navbar, theme, etc.).





Voice on home + about. Does it sound like you? If any sentence makes you cringe, mark it.
Karyotype. It’s drawn — not a real photographic SKY karyotype. Easy to swap. Tell me if the proportions/colors feel right or if you’d rather have a real one (I can recommend sources).
The three “what I do” lines. Do they cover what you actually do, in your words?
The featured work order. Patient → clinician → review memo. Reasonable?
Headshot. Currently round, 220px, in the about page. Want it on the homepage too?
Lived-experience paragraph on the About page. Lean-in version is in there. Tone okay? Too much, not enough, just right?





Sample pages still look default-Quarto on the inside; we’ll style them once you bless the homepage direction.
The Safe Evolution and teaching-design samples mentioned on the work page — we’ll write those as new pieces.
Domain / deployment. Once you bless this, we promote quarto/ to be the root of the site (or move the Jekyll files into _legacy/) and update GitHub Pages settings.
A real karyotype image (if you want one).

title: Redesigning a failing course
text:
Course redesign · Higher education
    Redesigning a failing course
    A flipped, OER-based rebuild of General Genetics that took the drop/fail/withdraw rate from 39% to under 5% — and held there for three consecutive years.
    
      Instructional systems design
      Data-driven iteration
      Equity-centered design
      Open educational resources
      Program management
      Genetics expertise
    
  

  
    The problem
    General Genetics at Oklahoma State had a nearly 40% drop/fail/withdraw rate. Students were failing in large numbers, the course relied on an expensive commercial textbook, and assessment was high-stakes exam-dependent — a structure the discipline-based education research literature consistently shows disadvantages underrepresented students.
  

  
    What I did
    I redesigned the course from the ground up using evidence from the learning sciences. I built a complete asynchronous content library — original short-form video lectures, embedded formative assessment questions, and open educational resources — that replaced the commercial textbook entirely. Weekly active-learning sessions targeted the specific conceptual bottlenecks where students consistently got lost: ploidy, meiosis, gene regulation.
    Assessment moved from high-stakes exams to mastery-based: two-attempt quizzes, homework revision opportunities, and synthesis reflections. Across eight concurrent sections, structured TA mentorship kept delivery consistent.
  

  
    The outcome

    
      
        
          39%
          →
          <5%
        
        Drop/fail/withdraw rate before and after the redesign — sustained over three consecutive years.
      
      
        
          200+
        
        Students per semester, across 8 concurrent sections, with a fully original content library.
      
    

    The redesign was recognized with an Oklahoma Regents for Higher Education OER Grant, and students nominated the course for the Arts & Sciences Distinguished Teacher Award in consecutive years. Students say:

    "This was one of the most well thought out courses I have ever taken."

    "I now have a new standard for which my future classes should be like."
  

  
    What I built

    
      
        
      
      
        Live website · Interactive syllabus
        Interactive General Genetics syllabus
        A student-facing syllabus built so students can find what they actually need — what to do each week, where to do it, what gets graded — without parsing a 12-page PDF. Includes expectations, accommodations, assessment policy, and instructional team.
        jwiggi18.github.io/gengen_syllabus ↗
      
    

    
      
        Live website · Open educational resource · In progress
        Open-access General Genetics content
        A growing open-access companion library that replaces the commercial textbook — units on genomes, chromosomes, ploidy, prions, and more, written from scratch and freely usable by other instructors. Built in Quarto with downloadable PDFs alongside the web version.
        jwiggi18.github.io/course_materials ↗

title: Clinical Exome and Genome Sequencing: What the Results Can and Can’t Tell You
text:
Clinician-facing scientific communication · Clinical genomics
    Clinical Exome and Genome Sequencing: What the Results Can and Can't Tell You
    A technical brief for healthcare providers on interpreting exome and genome sequencing results — what these tests reliably detect, where they fall short, and how to use findings responsibly in clinical practice.
    
      Clinician-facing translation
      Exome & genome sequencing
      Variant interpretation
      ACMG/AMP classification framework
      Clinical genomics
    
    Audience: Healthcare Providers, Clinical Geneticists, Genetic Counselors
  

  
    What these tests are
    Clinical exome sequencing targets the protein-coding regions of the genome, where the substantial majority of currently characterized disease-causing variants reside. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) extends coverage to non-coding regions, including regulatory sequences that contribute to disease in a subset of cases.
    The choice between exome and WGS should be driven by clinical context. Exome sequencing is appropriate as a first-line test for suspected single-gene or oligogenic conditions. WGS is worth considering when prior sequencing is negative and broader variant detection is clinically warranted, or when the clinical picture suggests non-coding involvement.
  

  
    What sequencing can detect — and what it misses
    Exome sequencing reliably detects single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions and deletions (indels) in protein-coding regions. WGS extends this to non-coding regions and improves sensitivity for some structural variants, but neither technology captures all disease-relevant variation.

    
      What current sequencing consistently misses or undercharacterizes
      
        Large structural variants and copy number variants (though some labs add CNV analysis)
        Repeat expansions (e.g., Fragile X, Huntington's, myotonic dystrophy)
        Mosaic variants, particularly at low allele frequency
        Variants in regions of low sequence complexity or high homology
      
    
  

  A negative sequencing result does not exclude a genetic etiology. It means the test didn't find a variant it was designed and powered to detect — which is not the same thing.

  
    Interpreting variant classifications
    Clinical laboratories classify variants using the ACMG/AMP five-tier framework, incorporating population frequency, functional data, segregation, and prior clinical observations:
    
      Pathogenic / Likely pathogenic — consistent with a genetic diagnosis when aligned with the patient's phenotype
      Variant of uncertain significance (VUS) — insufficient evidence to classify as pathogenic or benign; should not drive clinical decisions or cascade testing
      Likely benign / Benign — not expected to contribute to disease
    
    Two points worth emphasizing in clinical practice. First, VUS is not a diagnosis. Recommending predictive testing for family members based solely on a VUS finding is not supported by current guidelines and should be avoided. Second, classifications are not permanent — they reflect the current state of the evidence and may be reclassified as data accumulate. A VUS from three years ago is worth reassessing.
  

  
    Phenotype drives interpretation
    Detailed, accurate phenotypic information isn't optional — it's how variant interpretation gets traction. Prioritization algorithms weight variants against the clinical picture; a variant that looks unremarkable in a generic patient may become the leading candidate once the phenotype is specific.
    Incomplete or nonspecific phenotypic data produces more uncertain results and more VUS returns.
  

  The most common bottleneck in diagnostic sequencing workflows is not the sequencing — it's the phenotypic information available at the time of analysis.

  
    Using results in practice
    Sequencing results are most useful as part of a broader diagnostic strategy, not as a standalone answer. Clinical interpretation should integrate sequencing findings with phenotype, family history, and any prior test results. For pathogenic or likely pathogenic findings, referral to genetic counseling is appropriate to discuss implications for the patient and family members, including cascade testing.
    For inconclusive results, the most useful thing a clinician can do is document the specific phenotypic information that informed the test order and communicate it clearly to the laboratory. Many reanalyses yield results that initial analysis missed, not because the sequencing changed, but because the phenotypic input did.
  

  
    What to communicate to patients
    A few points that frequently require explicit discussion:
    
      A negative result is not a clean bill of genetic health. It means the test didn't find what it was looking for.
      VUS findings are common and are not diagnoses. Families should not make major medical decisions based on a VUS alone.
      Results can change over time. Patients should be encouraged to follow up with their provider or genetic counselor if they haven't heard back about a VUS result after a year or two.
      Sequencing has implications for family members, which is worth discussing before testing, not only after.

title: My Details
text:
Jodie Wiggins, PhD



  There is no knowledge that is not power.
  — Ralph Waldo Emerson

Making the power that is inherent in knowledge accessible is what I do.
My background is in genetics and evolutionary biology, specifically, a PhD plus over a decade of university teaching, but what I actually spend my time on is harder to categorize: designing the structures that help people understand genuinely difficult things. That might mean a flipped course that took a 39% failure rate to under 5%. Or a cross-disciplinary educator workshop that succeeded so thoroughly it surprised the people who commissioned it. Or a suite of original videos, active learning sessions, and assessment frameworks built from scratch because the existing materials weren’t good enough.
I think carefully about where people get lost and I design backward from that. I’m most useful when the problem is we have complex information and the people who need it aren’t getting it. That could be a content problem, a structure problem, or sometimes a trust problem. The core of addressing all three is curiosity.
Curiosity is my superpower.


I hold a PhD in integrative biology, working in genetics and evolutionary biology, and have over a decade of university teaching at Oklahoma State where I’m currently a Teaching Associate Professor. I also taught K–12 science for three years before that. I read the discipline-based education research literature. It is difficult to narrow down who to mention but Eyler, Ambrose et al., Blum, Theobald et al., McGuire, and Lang tend to sit at the top of the stack. I’ve continued my training in instructional design for adult learners, learning measurement, culturally responsive pedagogy (Smithsonian), open educational resources, science communication summits, and program management.
Technically, I’m fluent in R and Python — particularly for data visualization and analysis — and across the modern Markdown / Quarto / GitHub Pages publishing stack. I’ve coordinated research teams, led multi-section instructional operations at scale, and built educational programs from scratch.



I rebuilt our 8-section General Genetics course from the ground up: flipped, OER-based, evidence-driven. Three years later, the results are still holding. I’m now leveraging that to redesign our Introductory Biology course.

  
    
      39%
      →
      <5%
    
    Drop/fail/withdraw rate in General Genetics, before and after the redesign. Three consecutive years and counting.
  
  
    
      2,000+
    
    Students per year in Introductory Biology — the next course on my redesign list.
  

Adjacent to that: I co-founded our department’s Community of Practice, helped write Safe Evolution — the code of conduct for the Society for the Study of Evolution and partner societies — serve on our department’s AI Integration Team, and mentor K–8 students at Prairie Wood Forest School.
Before higher ed I was a certified K–12 science teacher. Before that I was a kid who couldn’t stop asking questions about how things worked.



After a decade in academia, I want to do this work somewhere it lives closer to where scientific information actually meets people’s lives. Medical communications. Scientific content strategy. Patient education. Editorial leadership.
Same skills, different impact.



I’ve also navigated the medical system as a complex patient — hEDS, MCAS, dysautonomia. The power of my knowledge saved my life.
I understand, from the other side of the chart, what it costs when scientific information isn't accessible to the people who need it most.
That perspective shapes how I write for patients, providers, and caregivers and the kind of work I want to do next.



Roles where the work is substantive, the team is collaborative, and the mission is real.
Full-time scientific content roles, content strategy and editorial leadership, freelance medical and patient communications — and conversations that don’t fit any of those boxes.

title: Exome and Genome Sequencing: A Guide for Patients and Families
text:
Patient & advocate education · Plain language translation · Clinical genomics
    Exome and Genome Sequencing: A Guide for Patients and Families
    What these tests look for, what they reliably find, where they fall short, and what to do when results are uncertain — written for patients, families, and advocates navigating the genetic testing process.
    
      Plain language translation
      Patient education
      Clinical genomics
      VUS communication
      Accessible science writing
    
    Audience: Patients, families, and patient advocates
  

  
    What these tests are
    Exome and genome sequencing are genetic tests that read your DNA to look for changes that might explain a health condition.
    Your DNA contains instructions your body uses to build proteins and regulate how cells work. Changes in those instructions — called variants — can sometimes cause disease. Most disease-causing variants identified to date sit in protein-coding regions of the genome: these are what exome sequencing looks at. Whole genome sequencing extends coverage to non-coding regions — areas that regulate gene activity — which matters in a subset of cases where the disease-causing change is in those regulatory regions rather than in a coding gene.
    Both tests are typically ordered when a condition is suspected to have a genetic cause, especially after more targeted testing hasn't provided an answer.
  

  
    What sequencing can detect — and what it misses
    These tests reliably find small DNA changes: single-letter typos in the genetic code, and small insertions or deletions. What they consistently miss:

    
      
        Large structural rearrangements and copy number changes — unless the lab has added specific analysis for these
        Repeat expansions — the type of mutation behind conditions like Fragile X, Huntington's disease, and myotonic dystrophy
        Mosaic changes — variants present in only some cells, not all, which can occur at low enough levels to be invisible
        Regions of the genome that are difficult to sequence accurately due to repetitive structure
      
    
  

  A negative result means the test didn't find a variant it was designed to find. It doesn't mean your symptoms aren't real or don't have a genetic basis. It means the answer, if there is one, is somewhere the test didn't look — or isn't findable with current technology.

  
    Understanding your results
    Clinical labs classify genetic variants into five categories based on how much evidence exists linking them to disease:

    
      Pathogenic / Likely pathogenic — a variant with strong evidence of causing disease, consistent with your specific medical situation. This is the result that leads to a diagnosis.
      Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) — a change where the current evidence isn't sufficient to say whether it causes disease. This is not a diagnosis. It is an open question.
      Likely benign / Benign — a variant not expected to contribute to disease.
    

    The category that confuses people most is VUS. Getting a VUS result is common — particularly in exome and genome sequencing, which cast a wide net and pick up many variants with unknown significance.
  

  A VUS should not drive clinical decisions on its own. That includes decisions about surgery, screening, or whether family members should be tested.

  
    A few other things to know about VUS results:
    
      VUS classifications change. A variant that's uncertain today may be reclassified — as pathogenic or as benign — as more data accumulate. Labs sometimes recontact patients when this happens, but not always. If you received a VUS result more than a year or two ago, it's worth asking your provider or genetic counselor to check whether the classification has been updated.
      Family members don't need to be tested for a VUS just because you have one. That changes if and when the VUS is reclassified as pathogenic.
    
  

  
    When results don't explain your symptoms
    A negative result — where the lab doesn't identify a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant — is the most common outcome of diagnostic sequencing. It doesn't mean your workup is over.
    Some paths forward after an inconclusive result:
    
      Re-analysis — as databases grow and more variants are characterized, labs can reanalyze existing sequencing data with updated information. Many results that were initially inconclusive become informative with reanalysis. Your provider can request this.
      Additional testing — sequencing misses certain variant types. Depending on your clinical picture, your provider might recommend tests that target what sequencing doesn't capture.
      Specialist referral — if you haven't already seen a clinical geneticist or genetic counselor, this is the right time.
    
  

  
    What genetic results mean for family members
    Many genetic variants are inherited. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic result in you may be relevant for biological relatives — parents, siblings, children — who could be at increased risk. This is called cascade testing.
    A genetic counselor can help you understand which family members might benefit from testing, how to approach those conversations, and what testing options exist for relatives. VUS findings, as noted above, should not trigger cascade testing unless and until they are reclassified.
  

  
    Questions to ask your provider

    Before testing:
    
      Why is exome or genome sequencing being recommended for my situation rather than a more targeted test?
      What kinds of results are most likely, and what would each mean for my care?
      What won't this test be able to tell me?
      Are there implications for my family members regardless of the result?
    

    After receiving results:
    
      What does this result mean specifically for my diagnosis and care plan?
      If the result is a VUS: what's the process for following up as the evidence evolves?
      If the result is negative: what are the next steps? Is reanalysis or additional testing worth pursuing?
      Should any family members be tested based on this finding?
    
  

  
    FAQ

    

    Will these tests always give me a diagnosis?
    No. Diagnostic rates vary by condition, but even in the best circumstances, exome and genome sequencing identifies a definitive genetic cause in roughly 25–35% of cases where a genetic condition is suspected. Many results are inconclusive or negative, especially on first analysis. That number improves with reanalysis over time.

    

    Why might my doctor recommend genome sequencing instead of exome sequencing?
    Usually because prior testing — including exome sequencing — didn't find an answer, or because the clinical picture suggests a non-coding variant might be involved. Genome sequencing is more expensive and generates more data, so it's typically reserved for situations where the broader coverage is warranted.

    

    How will I know if my VUS result gets reclassified?
    You may not be notified automatically — it depends on the lab and your provider's practices. The safest approach is to ask your provider or genetic counselor to check on any VUS result that's more than one to two years old.

    

    Who is the right person to explain my results to me?
    A genetic counselor. Genetic counselors are specifically trained to translate sequencing results into plain language, explain what findings mean for your health and your family, and help you decide on next steps. If you don't have one, ask your ordering provider for a referral.

title: Scientific Content Review: BRCA1/2 and Hereditary Cancer Risk
text:
Scientific content leadership · Medical communications · Oncology
    Scientific Content Review: BRCA1/2 and Hereditary Cancer Risk
    An internal scientific review of an educational slide deck for oncology teams — assessing accuracy, interpretive risk, and alignment between evidence and clinical claims. Five issues identified. Four required revision; one addition recommended.
    
      Scientific oversight
      Interpretive risk assessment
      BRCA1/2 · Hereditary cancer
      Variant classification (ACMG/AMP)
      Somatic vs. germline testing
      Medical communications
    
  

  
    Internal Review Memo (Anonymized) · Reviewer: Jodie Wiggins, Ph.D. · Role: Scientific Content Lead

    Note: This report would follow only after a collaborative and collegeal conversation with the relevant team members

    What was reviewed and why
    This deck was developed to support oncology teams in understanding BRCA1/2 testing indications, result interpretation, and patient management. It's intended for educational use at tumor board and CME settings.
    The science in this deck is largely sound. The problems are interpretive — places where the language slightly outruns what the evidence supports, or where a technically accurate statement will be read by a clinician as something it doesn't quite mean.
  

  Those are the issues most likely to cause harm in practice, and the ones this review focuses on.

  
    Reviewed content (anonymized)
    Representative slides and claims assessed in this review:
    
      Slides 1–2: Overview of germline BRCA1/2 testing indications and population prevalence
      Slide 4: Penetrance estimates — "Women with pathogenic BRCA1 variants have a 72% lifetime risk of breast cancer and a 44% lifetime risk of ovarian cancer"
      Slide 6: VUS management — "Variants of uncertain significance should be disclosed to patients, and at-risk family members may consider predictive testing based on this finding"
      Slide 7: Somatic and germline testing — "Tumor BRCA testing identifies patients who may benefit from PARP inhibitor therapy and can reveal hereditary risk"
      Slide 9: Mechanism — homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) and synthetic lethality with PARP inhibition
      Slide 10: Patient communication and referral to genetic counseling
    
  

  
    What's working
    Outline, Visuals, and Structure.  The outline of the slide deck clearly guides participants through relevant background information without over-explaining, uses white space and visuals well. Overall structure is excellent. 
    Slide 9 (HRD mechanism) is the strongest slide in the deck. The explanation of homologous recombination deficiency and the mechanistic basis for PARP inhibitor synthetic lethality is accurate, appropriately detailed for the audience, and well structured. The figure does real explanatory work — it's not decorative. Keep it as-is, fantastic.
    The referral recommendation on Slide 10 is correct, clearly stated, and the perfect closing: all patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic BRCA1/2 findings should be referred to genetic counseling. No changes needed there.
  

  
    Issues requiring revision

    

    1. Recommended addition: an orientation slide on variant classification
    The deck makes regular reference to pathogenic variants, VUS findings, and clinical decision thresholds — but never establishes what those terms mean for the audience. Oncologists who don't routinely interpret genomic results may know the vocabulary without understanding the clinical weight attached to each category. A clinician who doesn't know that a VUS should not drive clinical decisions may not catch the significance of that guidance when it appears later on Slide 6.
    The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology established the standard five-tier classification framework for sequence variants in Richards et al. (2015, Genetics in Medicine 17:405–424). An orientation slide early in the deck — before the VUS and penetrance material — would give the clinical audience the interpretive frame they need to use the rest of the content correctly.

    Recommended addition

    

      
        ACMG/AMP 2015 Framework
        Variant Classification: What Each Result Means for Clinical Care
      

      
      
        ✕
        
          
            Pathogenic
            Meets established criteria for disease causation.
          
          Can be used in clinical decision making
        
      

      
      
        △
        
          
            Likely Pathogenic
            >90% certainty of pathogenicity. Sufficient to inform decisions with supporting clinical evidence.
          
          Can inform clinical decision making
        
      

      
      
        ?
        
          
            Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS)
          
          Insufficient or conflicting evidence to classify as pathogenic or benign.
          ⚠ Should NOT be used in clinical decision making
        
      

      
      
        ◎
        
          
            Likely Benign
            >90% certainty of benign effect. Not expected to be the cause of the patient's condition.
          
          Not expected to contribute to disease
        
      

      
      
        ✓
        
          
            Benign
            Sufficient evidence of benign effect. Not the cause of the patient's disorder.
          
          Not the cause of the patient's disorder
        
      

      
        Richards et al. 2015, Genetics in Medicine 17:405–424 · Classifications may be updated as evidence accumulates
      

    

    This slide belongs near the beginning of the deck, before any discussion of specific test results. The VUS misuse problem flagged in issue 3 below is harder to catch without this frame in place.

    

    2. Penetrance figure is presented as a definitive and there is no citation
    Slide 4 states: "Women with pathogenic BRCA1 variants have a 72% lifetime risk of breast cancer and a 44% lifetime risk of ovarian cancer."
    The 72% figure comes from a specific study — likely Kuchenbaecker et al. (2017, JAMA) who used a prospective cohort of known carriers or other clinical cohort data. The broader literature spans roughly 45% to over 80% for BRCA1 breast cancer risk depending on population, ascertainment method, and cohort (e.g. Antoniou et al. 2003 American Journal of Human Genetics 72:1117–1130 - see below for more references) and better represents known uncertainty. Studies using clinical cohorts historically overestimate penetrance relative to population-based cohorts.
    This matters clinically: a clinician or patient who hears "72%" may interpret that as precision the number doesn't have.

    
      
        
          72%
          →
          45–85%
        
        BRCA1 lifetime breast cancer risk: the point estimate on the slide vs. the actual range in the literature. Presenting the point estimate alone overstates the precision of the evidence.
      
    

    Recommended revision

    
      
        BRCA1 pathogenic variants are associated with substantially elevated lifetime risks of breast and ovarian cancer.
      
      
        
          Risk estimates vary by study methodology and cohort.
        
        
          Current data suggest lifetime breast cancer risks of approximately:
          
            Breast Cancer
            45–85%
          
          
            Ovarian Cancer
            40–60%
          
        
      
      
        Patients should discuss individual risk in the context of personal and family history with a genetic counselor.
      
    

    Cite the source for whatever figures you use. If the deck is going into a CME context, the citation belongs on the slide, not in an appendix.

    

    3. Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) management recommendation is incorrect
    Slide 6 states: "Variants of uncertain significance should be disclosed to patients, and at-risk family members may consider predictive testing based on this finding."

    
      
      A VUS, by definition, has insufficient evidence to classify as pathogenic or benign.
    

     It is important to remember that we have single nucleotide changes throughout our genomes that have no clinical relevance. Any change is often assumed to be clinically significant. This is not the case. Future research could associate a VUS with disease or it could be benign. 
    
    Recommending that family members pursue predictive testing based on a VUS treats an unresolved finding as if it carries clinical weight it doesn't yet have. American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines are explicit: VUS findings should not be used in clinical decision making (Richards et al. 2015 Genetics in Medicine). Genetic counselors know this, but an oncologist reading this slide may not.

    
      Recommended revision
      "Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) should be disclosed to patients and documented in the medical record. VUS findings should not be used as the basis for predictive testing in at-risk family members or to guide clinical management. Patients should be informed that VUS classifications may be updated as scientific evidence evolves, and that they should follow up with their ordering provider or genetic counselor to check on any VUS result that is more than one to two years old."
    

    

    4. Somatic BRCA testing does not establish germline status
    Slide 7 states: "Tumor BRCA testing identifies patients who may benefit from PARP inhibitor therapy and can reveal hereditary risk."
    The first clause is correct. The second is not — or more precisely, it's accurate in a narrow technical sense but will almost certainly be misread.
    Somatic (tumor-based) BRCA testing identifies variants present in the tumor. A BRCA variant detected in tumor tissue may reflect an underlying germline mutation, but it may also be a somatic mutation acquired during tumor development. Tumor testing cannot reliably distinguish between these. The slide as written will lead some clinicians to treat a positive tumor BRCA result as evidence of hereditary risk — which is only sometimes true, and is never confirmed without germline testing.
    Patients whose germline status is not confirmed following a positive tumor BRCA result may not receive appropriate genetic counseling or cascade testing referrals for family members. Let's clear that up.

    Recommended revision

    

      
        Slide 7 — Recommended revision
        Understanding BRCA Test Results: Somatic vs. Germline
      

      

        
          Somatic (Tumor) Testing

          
            
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
              ✦
              
              
              ✦
              
              
            
            Mutation present in some cells only
          

          Can tell you
          
            ✓
            Whether the tumor carries a BRCA variant that may predict PARP inhibitor response
          
          Cannot tell you
          
            ✕
            Whether the variant is inherited or acquired in the tumor
          
          
            ✕
            Whether family members are at increased risk
          
        

        
          Germline Testing

          
            
              
              
              ✦
              
              
              ✦
              
              
              ✦
              
              
              ✦
              
              
              ✦
              
              
              ✦
            
            Mutation present in every cell
          

          Can tell you
          
            ✓
            Whether the BRCA variant is inherited — present in every cell from birth
          
          
            ✓
            Whether family members may be at increased risk and should consider cascade testing
          
          
            ✓
            Long-term surveillance and management decisions for the patient
          
        

      

      
        A positive tumor BRCA result warrants referral to genetic counseling to discuss germline testing — it does not confirm hereditary risk on its own.
      

    

    

    5. Minor: limitations are buried
    The deck addresses testing limitations — sensitivity, VUS prevalence, the fact that a negative result doesn't exclude a genetic etiology — but these points appear on Slide 8, after the patient management recommendations on Slides 6–7. Clinicians reading a slide deck in a clinical setting often don't make it to Slide 8.
    The limitations that most directly affect how clinicians will act — the VUS caveat and the somatic/germline distinction — should be surfaced at the point of use, not consolidated at the end. The information is in the deck; it's just not where it will be seen.
  

  Four of the five issues above involve claims that are technically defensible but will predictably be read as something more certain or more actionable than the evidence supports. That's the category of error most worth catching in scientific review.

  
    Summary
    The fixes are targeted. The deck doesn't need to be rebuilt — it needs a variant classification orientation slide added near the top, the penetrance slide to carry its uncertainty honestly, the VUS slide to clearly state what the standard of care actually is, and the somatic/germline distinction to be explicit rather than implied.

    This memo is an anonymized example of scientific content oversight for educational and portfolio purposes. The slide content described is representative, not drawn from an actual product or client.
  

  
    References
    
      
        Richards S, Aziz N, Bale S, et al. Standards and guidelines for the interpretation of sequence variants: a joint consensus recommendation of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology. Genet Med. 2015;17(5):405–424.
        Source for the ACMG/AMP five-tier variant classification framework (pathogenic, likely pathogenic, VUS, likely benign, benign) and clinical guidance on variant use in practice. The VUS management and cascade testing guidance referenced throughout this review derives from this framework.
      
      
        Kuchenbaecker KB, Hopper JL, Barnes DR, et al. Risks of breast, ovarian, and contralateral breast cancer for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carriers. JAMA. 2017;317(23):2402–2416.
        Prospective cohort of known BRCA1/2 carriers; source of the 72% BRCA1 breast cancer risk estimate used on Slide 4.
      
      
        Antoniou A, Pharoah PDP, Narod S, et al. Average risks of breast and ovarian cancer associated with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations detected in case series unselected for family history. Am J Hum Genet. 2003;72(5):1117–1130.
        Meta-analysis of 22 studies not selected for family history; BRCA1 cumulative breast cancer risk ~65% by age 70. Frequently cited lower-end estimate from a rigorous source.
      
      
        Chen S, Parmigiani G. Meta-analysis of BRCA1 and BRCA2 penetrance. J Clin Oncol. 2007;25(11):1329–1333. PMID 17416853.
        Meta-analytic mean cumulative BRCA1 breast cancer risk at age 70: 57% (95% CI 47–66%). Provides the most systematic lower-bound estimate across the literature and is the basis for the 45–85% range noted in this review.
      
      
        Brohet et al. Breast and ovarian cancer risks in a large series of clinically ascertained families with a high proportion of BRCA1 and BRCA2 Dutch founder mutations. J Med Genet. 2014. doi:10.1136/jmedgenet-2013-101974.
        Dutch founder mutation cohort; cumulative BRCA1 breast cancer risk by age 70: 45% (95% CI 36–52%). Among the lowest point estimates in the literature; illustrates how population and ascertainment affect penetrance figures.

title: Building an education program
text:
Program design & launch · Federally-funded research initiative
    Building an education program
    Ground up build of an education and outreach division for a federally-funded phylogenetics initiative — including a researcher-educator workshop model with results that surprised the people who commissioned it.
    
      Program design and launch
      Cross-functional team leadership
      Workshop facilitation
      Instructional technology development
      Stakeholder management
    
  

  
    The problem
    A federally-funded phylogenetics research initiative had no education or outreach component. The science was significant and publicly funded, but inaccessible to educators and the broader public. No one on the team had built this kind of program before.
  

  
    What I did
    I created the vision, strategy, and structure for an education division from scratch. I built and coordinated a distributed cross-functional team — computer scientists, phylogenetics researchers, and educators across multiple institutions — and developed interactive web-based phylogenetic learning tools in R, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.
    The centerpiece was the inaugural subject-specialist/educator collaborative workshop: a model that brought researchers and teachers together to co-produce educational resources from large-scale biological datasets. 

   
    Designing the workshop meant designing the structure that would let two professional cultures actually do work together — rather than presenting at one another.
  
  

  
    The outcome

    
      
        
          100%
        
        Positive participant feedback from the inaugural researcher-educator workshop.
      
      
        
          < 1 yr
        
        From scoping to a launched program division, with a working workshop model and a published OER suite.
      
    

    The workshop produced a suite of open educational resources that are still publicly available. Organizers described the outcome as unlike anything they had seen before — the model demonstrated that researchers and educators could productively co-create in a structured collaborative format, a result that surprised the broader team.
  

  
    What I built

    
      
        
      
      
        Live website · Workshop deliverable hub
        phyloEd
        The site I built to host every educational resource produced by the workshop — interactive learning websites, full lesson plans aligned to NGSS, and teacher-facing quick-start guides. Co-developed with public-school teachers and phylogenetics researchers.
        jwiggi18.github.io/phyloEd ↗
      
    

    
      
        
      
      
        Live website · Flagship interactive build
        History of Earth
        An interactive learning module connecting geologic time, climate change, and biological evolution — co-developed with researchers Brian O'Meara, Dave Bapst, and Luna Sanchez Reyes alongside public-school teachers Nellie Johnson, Kellee Shuttleworth, and Cara Stephens. Maps to multiple NGSS standards across middle and high school.
        historyofearth.net ↗
      
    

    
      
        
      
      
        Parent project · NSF-funded research initiative
        Phylotastic
        The parent research initiative — a multi-institution NSF-funded effort to make the Tree of Life computable, citable, and ready-to-use. I built the education and outreach division, contributed code and R packages to the broader infrastructure, and wired up API access for the educator-facing tools.
        phylotastic.org ↗
      
    

    Source code for the phyloEd hub lives at github.com/jwiggi18/phyloEd. Phylotastic's open-source code, including R packages and API services, is at github.com/phylotastic.

title: What national data says about the STEM completion gap
text:
Data analysis · Public dataset · Higher education
    What national data says about the STEM completion gap
    A reproducible analysis of U.S. bachelor's degree completion in STEM fields using public IPEDS data. We know completion gaps exist. This analysis seeks to explore where the gap opens, who it traps, and what the institutional data can reliabily tell us about why.
    
      Public dataset (IPEDS / NCES)
      Descriptive & longitudinal analysis
      Equity-stratified outcomes
      Data wrangling at scale
      Python · pandas · matplotlib
      Reproducible reporting (Quarto)
    
  

  
    Why this question
    I spent years redesigning single STEM gateway courses and watched what shifted when the design changed, and what didn't. That's the view from inside one classroom. The view from outside it at the level of every U.S. degree-granting institution, across almost a decade is what this analysis goes after.
    The question: where in the STEM bachelor's degree pipeline does the equity gap sit, and how stable is the pattern across fields and institution types? 
    A gap reported as a single national number can obscure actionable nuance. A gap broken out by instructional programs (CIP field) and institution sector tells you where action can have impact and where the national average is smoothing informative variation.
  

  
    The data
    All from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), maintained by the National Center for Education Statistics. Public, free, no registration required.
    
      Completions (C_A survey) — degree counts by 6-digit CIP code, award level, race/ethnicity, and gender, by institution and year. Bachelor's degrees = AWLEVEL=5, first majors only (MAJORNUM=1).
      Institutional Characteristics (HD) — sector, Carnegie classification, control type. The grouping variables that make the rest meaningful.
    
    Scope: U.S. Title IV degree-granting institutions. Years: 2013, 2015–2017 (2014 data excluded — file truncated at row 253,038, reducing institution coverage by ~28%; the artifact produced a spurious one-year dip that is not a real trend). STEM definition: NSF STEM CIP crosswalk (2-digit families: 11, 14, 15, 26, 27, 40, 41, 03). Health professions (CIP 51) reported separately — including them substantially shifts the gendered patterns in the data.
    ~2,600–2,800 institutions per year. ~78,000–82,000 institution × CIP × demographic rows per year after filtering to bachelor's level.
  

  
    What I expected to find — and what the data said
    I wrote the expected pattern before running the analysis. Without that discipline, every result looks obvious in retrospect.
    What I expected: overall STEM bachelor's counts rising; Black and Hispanic students underrepresented in STEM relative to their share of all bachelor's degrees; the gap larger and more stable in engineering and physical sciences than in biology or CS; a sector effect showing the gap concentrated at doctoral-granting institutions.
    What I found: the first two confirmed, the third partially, the fourth not the way I expected.
  

  
    Finding 1: The gap is persistent, not closing
    The core measure: STEM degrees as a share of each group's total bachelor's degrees earned. If a group earns 10% of all bachelor's in STEM, that 10% is their STEM share. It controls for differences in group size and total enrollment growth.

    
      
    

    Black students earned 5.7% of their bachelor's degrees in STEM in 2013. By 2017 that was 6.4% — a 0.7 percentage point gain over four years. White students went from 8.6% to 9.9% over the same period. The gap between Black and White STEM share was 2.9 percentage points in 2013 and 3.5 points in 2017. It grew while both numbers rose.
    Hispanic students fared somewhat better — 7.3% to 8.5%, tracking closer to White students — but still below. Asian students are consistently the highest at 15–17%, and rising.
    The trend lines are all moving in the same direction. That matters: it means overall STEM enrollment is expanding and pulling everyone along. It does not mean the gap is closing. The four lines are not converging.
  

  
    Finding 2: Who's actually driving the growth
    Counts indexed to 2013 = 100 show how each group's STEM bachelor's production grew over the window.

    
      
    

    Hispanic STEM bachelor's completions grew 56% between 2013 and 2017, from 28,633 to 44,775 — nearly four times the rate for White students (+15%). Asian completions grew 29%. Black completions grew 16%, just barely outpacing White growth.
    The Hispanic growth is real and notable. It shows up in the STEM share chart too — the Hispanic line is the one actually closing distance on White. But even at +56% growth, Hispanic students started from a lower absolute base (28,633 in 2013 vs. 197,256 for White), and their STEM share in 2017 (8.5%) is still below the White rate in 2013 (8.6%).
    The Black growth story is the harder one: +16% raw growth over four years, but this is slightly above the overall STEM completion growth rate (~24%), so it isn't translating into a closing gap.
  

  
    Finding 3: The field-level breakdown is where the national average stops being useful
    The aggregated STEM share hides enormous variation. Biology and computer science behave nothing like engineering and physical sciences.

    
      
    

    A few things stand out:
    Computer science is the wrong kind of outlier. Black students had 10.7% of CS bachelor's in 2013 — the highest of any non-biology STEM field. By 2017 that had dropped to 8.4%, while the field as a whole grew 40%. CS added about 20,000 bachelor's degrees between 2013 and 2017; the share of those going to Black students fell. The field expanded and Black representation shrank within it.
    Biology is the most diverse major STEM field by a wide margin. Black (7.6%) and Hispanic (13.1%) both have their highest representation in biological sciences by 2017, and the Hispanic number represents a significant gain from 9.7% in 2013. Biology is also the largest single STEM field by degree count (118,856 bachelor's in 2017), which makes this meaningful at scale.
    Engineering is nearly unchanged. Black representation in engineering went from 4.0% in 2013 to 3.7% in 2017, while engineering added about 30,000 annual bachelor's degrees. Flat to declining share in a growing field.
    Hispanic students are gaining across the board. Every field shows Hispanic growth from 2013 to 2017, with the largest gains in biology (+3.4 pp), physical sciences (+3.0 pp), and engineering (+1.7 pp).
    The field-level variation matters for interpreting the national number. "STEM" isn't one pipeline — it's seven substantially different ones, with substantially different representation patterns. An intervention designed for engineering won't transfer directly to biology, and vice versa.
  

  
    Finding 4: Public vs. private nonprofit — the sector effect is real but consistent

    
      
    

    Public institutions show consistently higher STEM shares across all racial/ethnic groups — roughly 1–1.5 percentage points higher than private nonprofit institutions for Black and Hispanic students. This is partly a size effect: public institutions are larger, enroll more students, and tend to have more engineering programs. But the relative order of groups is the same at both sector types, and the gap between groups is similar.
    What this tells you: the equity gap is not primarily a sector artifact. The same pattern shows up whether you're looking at a public research university or a private liberal arts college. It's not explained by where students are enrolled.
  

  
    Where the data stops being able to answer the question
    IPEDS is institutional and aggregate. It counts degrees awarded — it doesn't record who left, when, or why. The gap this analysis documents is a completion gap. The attrition gap — at what point in the sequence are students leaving STEM? — requires different data. The BPS longitudinal survey and HSLS:09 cohort study are the right tools for that question; IPEDS isn't.
    A few other limits worth naming:
    The analysis uses HD2022 institutional characteristics to classify institutions across 2013–2017 data. Control type (public / private) is stable; Carnegie classification can shift as institutions grow. Carnegie-stratified results were excluded from the final writeup for this reason.
    The 2014 data file truncated during download (EOF error at row 253,038, reducing institution coverage by ~28%). Real-world data quality issues like this are normal in IPEDS work — the right call is to document them and exclude rather than silently include a corrupted year.
    The NSF STEM CIP crosswalk is documented and replicable, but "STEM" still does a lot of definitional work. Health professions (CIP 51) are excluded here; including them shifts the gendered patterns substantially and modestly shifts the racial/ethnic patterns as well.
  

  
    What I'd dig into next
    Extend to 2018–2023. This analysis covers 2013–2017; downloading additional years from the NCES complete data files would let the same code produce the full decade picture. The methodology is built for it.
    Institutional outliers. The institutions that close the gap — the ones whose patterns don't match their sector average — are the analytically interesting ones. A residual analysis would surface them. That's a more targeted analysis than this one, and the one that's actually useful for program design.
    Persistence vs. completion. IPEDS degrees-awarded data can't tell you when students left. Linking to BPS or HSLS:09 would let you ask: is the gap opening at entry into STEM majors, during gateway courses, or at the point of degree completion? Those are three different problems with three different levers.
    Field-level trends for 4-digit CIPs. Computer science (11) contains both traditional CS and information systems. Engineering (14) contains civil, mechanical, electrical, and chemical. The 2-digit aggregation used here is already informative, but 4-digit would show where within these fields the representation patterns are most uneven.
  

  
    The code
    Analysis in Python (pandas, matplotlib). Reproducible from raw IPEDS complete data files. The full analysis script is below; the figures directory and processed CSVs are in the repository.

    import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# STEM CIP families — NSF crosswalk (2-digit)
STEM_CIP_2DIGIT = {
    '03': 'Natural Resources & Conservation',
    '11': 'Computer & Information Sciences',
    '14': 'Engineering',
    '15': 'Engineering Technologies',
    '26': 'Biological & Biomedical Sciences',
    '27': 'Mathematics & Statistics',
    '40': 'Physical Sciences',
    '41': 'Science Technologies',
}

def load_year(year, data_dir):
    """Load one year of IPEDS C_A completions data.
    Filters to AWLEVEL=5 (bachelor's), MAJORNUM=1 (first major).
    Returns df with IS_STEM flag and CIP2 (2-digit) column.
    """
    path = f"{data_dir}/C{year}_A.csv"
    try:
        df = pd.read_csv(path, usecols=NEEDED_COLS, encoding='latin1')
    except Exception:
        # Fall back to Python engine for files with embedded quotes / EOF issues
        df = pd.read_csv(path, usecols=NEEDED_COLS, encoding='latin1',
                         engine='python', on_bad_lines='skip')

    df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()
    df = df[(df['AWLEVEL'] == 5) & (df['MAJORNUM'] == 1)].copy()
    df['CIP2']    = df['CIPCODE'].astype(str).str.split('.').str[0].str.zfill(2)
    df['IS_STEM'] = df['CIP2'].isin(STEM_CIP_2DIGIT.keys())
    df['YEAR']    = year

    # Imputation-suppressed cells are coded as 0 in count columns
    for col in DEMO_COLS:
        df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce').fillna(0).astype(int)

    return df

# Load 2013, 2015–2017 (2014 excluded: file truncated, ~28% of institutions missing)
frames = [load_year(yr, DATA_DIR) for yr in [2013, 2015, 2016, 2017]]
df = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

# Merge with HD for institution type
hd = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/HD2022.csv",
                 usecols=['UNITID','CONTROL'], encoding='latin1')
df = df.merge(hd, on='UNITID', how='left')


    Data: IPEDS Completions Survey (C_A files) and Institutional Characteristics (HD), downloaded from the NCES complete data files at nces.ed.gov/ipeds/datacenter. All inputs public; no registration required. The full analysis script and figures are in the quarto/work/ directory of this repository.
